sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown: **No state trade license covers chimney work in Delaware — the gating credential is a tax/business license, not a skills exam.** STATE LAW: general and specialty contractors (masonry, roofing, etc.) do **not** sit for a state contractor exam. What Delaware requires is a **Division of Revenue contractor business license — 30 Del. C. § 2502(a)** ("Any person desiring to engage in business in this State as a contractor shall obtain a license upon making application to the Division of Revenue and paying a fee of $75"), renewed annually, plus a **gross-receipts license fee of 0.6472%** above a monthly deduction (§ 2502(c)); issuance requires proof of workers' compensation coverage and a Department of Labor certificate (§ 2502(b)). **Non-resident** contractors must post a **surety bond (or approved letter of credit) of 6% of the contract price on contracts of $20,000 or more** (aggregating within a calendar year), payable to the State — **30 Del. C. § 375** (Ch. 3, Subch. V — *not* Ch. 25). Separately, the **Delaware Contractor Registration Act, 19 Del. C. Ch. 36**, requires contractors performing construction services to register with the Department of Labor's Office of Contractor Registration (§ 3604) — a worker-misclassification measure, not a competence test; registration information is **not public** under FOIA (§ 3605(e)). The Division of Professional Regulation licenses only **electricians, plumbers, and HVACR** by exam — masonry/chimney is not among them *(DPR scope not re-read Sep 2026)*. Consumer-side duties for residential repair contractors come from the **DOJ Consumer Protection Unit's Home Improvement Services Regulation (Regulation 106, 27 DE Reg 254, effective Nov 1, 2023)**, adopted under the Consumer Fraud Act (6 Del. C. § 2513): complete written contracts listing material terms, a completion date or written explanation, no calling a binding contract an "estimate," no completion sign-off before work is finished, and notice of any § 4404 cancellation right. Its definition of "home improvement" — shared with the criminal **home improvement fraud statute, 11 Del. C. § 916** — expressly lists **"chimneys, fireplaces, stoves."** Public lookup: **Division of Revenue business-license search (revenue.delaware.gov/business-license-search/)**. So "licensed and bonded" in Delaware usually means *has a Revenue business license*, which attests tax registration — not flue competence.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Wide. A Delaware chimney contractor can be fully "licensed" (Division of Revenue) without ever demonstrating masonry or flue skill — the business license tests nothing about the work. Chimney sweeping and chimney repair sit on the **same** side of the line here: neither is a state-examined trade. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) and an independent inspection are the only real competence signal. NATIONAL STANDARD NFPA 211 fills the vacuum the state leaves open.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence; real, mandatory, names the chimney)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; real, mandatory, names the chimney
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: Delaware has a **mandatory** seller disclosure under the **Buyer Property Protection Act, 6 Del. C. § 2572** (disclosure of material defects) with the **property condition report at § 2573 and form contents at 6 Del. C. § 2578** (Buyer Property Protection Act, 6 Del. C. §§ 2570–2578). The statute itself does not mention chimneys; the **Delaware Real Estate Commission's Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report (form revision Aug 1, 2025)** does, in **Section XIV "Fireplace or Heating Stove," Qs 144–150**: number of fireplaces/stoves, fuel type, whether part of the original design, whether **"installed by a professional contractor or manufacturer's representative,"** "Are there any problems?", and **Q150 "When were the flues/chimneys last cleaned, serviced, or repaired?"** (dprfiles.delaware.gov/realestate/FINAL_DREC Sellers Disclosure for Real Property Condition Report 9_17_2024.pdf). *(Timing of delivery relative to the offer not re-read in Sep 2026.)* This is one of the few forms nationally that asks a *service-history* question about the flue. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: the **Consumer Fraud Act, 6 Del. C. § 2513** (unlawful practices), enforced by the DOJ Consumer Protection Unit, reaches deceptive home-repair practices. Door-knock work is separately governed by the **Home Solicitation Sales Act, 6 Del. C. Ch. 44 (§ 4404)**, giving buyers a **3-business-day right to cancel** any door-to-door sale of $25+ ("YOU, THE BUYER, MAY CANCEL THIS TRANSACTION AT ANY TIME PRIOR TO MIDNIGHT OF THE THIRD BUSINESS DAY"), with refunds due within 10 business days — the exact mechanic of chimney scare-sales. The DOJ Home Improvement Services Regulation requires contracts to disclose that § 4404 right where it applies, and 11 Del. C. § 916 treats noncompliance with Ch. 44 on a home improvement contract as prima facie evidence of intent for home improvement fraud. *(A 2024 bill — HB 427, 152nd GA — would have added a separate home-improvement cancel/deposit-cap subchapter to 6 Del. C. Ch. 36; it was substituted and **no such subchapter appears in the current code** — not law.)* Complaints: Delaware DOJ Consumer Protection.

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: STATE LAW/LOCAL: Delaware has **no single statewide residential building code enforced uniformly**; adoption and enforcement run through the three counties (**New Castle, Kent, Sussex**) and municipalities (Wilmington, Dover, Newark), most on an IRC base — **verify current IRC cycle per jurisdiction before publish.** Chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work where a building department exists; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. Sussex County's rapid-growth beach corridor and New Castle's older stock diverge in practice.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; NARROW — excludes owner-occupied homes)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; NARROW — excludes owner-occupied homes
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: **16 Del. C. Ch. 66C (§§ 6601C–6605C)** requires CO detectors, but **only in "lodging establishments"** — hotels, motels, apartments, multi-family, dorms, B&Bs, condos — that have a fossil-fuel appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage. **A private residence occupied by the owner is expressly excluded from "lodging establishment," so owner-occupied single-family homes are NOT covered by Delaware's CO statute.** Absence-as-finding: unlike NY/IL, Delaware has **no statewide CO requirement for owner-occupied dwellings** and no pre-sale CO certificate. Civil fine $100–$500 per offense for covered owners (§ 6605C). A permitted chimney job is still the natural moment to add alarms even where the law doesn't compel them.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. Not a material content section for DE.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Delaware **CONFIRMS the master finding.** With **no competence-based state license** for chimney work — just a Division of Revenue business license that tests tax registration, not masonry — the state compensates on the *sale* side: § 2572's **mandatory** disclosure form asks about the flue *by name* and even wants its **cleaning/service history**, one of the more specific chimney questions on any state form. That is the classic weak-license / strong-disclosure inversion. The oddball twist is the CO statute, which quietly **exempts owner-occupied homes**, so the very buyers the disclosure protects get no state CO mandate once they move in.
